info.body:
Adds an everyday garden task: switch a hose watering wand from Jet to Shower. A Melnor RelaxGrip 8-Pattern 16 in. pivot wand (404 mm, 0.30 kg, dry, no hose) lies on the bench; its head's dial clicks round eight spray patterns, held in each click by a sprung ball, and starts on Jet. One hand pinches the handle and keeps the wand from turning while the other pinches the dial's rim and turns it with the wrist, one click at a time, two clicks to Shower, then both let go. Turned with one hand only, the light round wand just rolls along with the dial and the pattern never changes; stopped short, the dial sits between two patterns. Full credit needs Shower in its click (within 5 degrees), the wand lying still on the bench and both hands clear for 1 s; Shower but still held scores 0.5, one click only (Center) 0.25.

The task runs through Isaac Lab-Arena and Inspect Robots. Dream-1 run: 0.0 (2,400 steps). Scripted demo: 1.0 (589 steps).

info.body:
The robot pulls out a wheeled suitcase's handle, the everyday move most people make every trip: an American Tourister Airconic Spinner 55/20 hard-shell cabin case (55 x 40 x 20 cm, 2.0 kg) lies flat on the bench, handle side up, its twin-tube telescopic handle closed. A release button in the grip works a lock pin in each rail; the pins lock the handle closed, at a first height (260 mm out) and at full height (520 mm out). One hand holds the case down; the other pinches the grip with one pad on the button, so the pinch keeps the button in and both pins clear, draws the handle out in one straight stroke past the first height to the stop, then lets the button back so both pins drop in. Letting the button up early leaves the handle at the first height; pinching beside the button leaves both pins in and the handle does not move. Full credit needs the handle locked at full height (520 +-3 mm, both pins in, button out), both grippers 5 cm clear for 1 s and the case within 50 mm and 10 degrees of where it lay; locked at full height with the case dragged further scores 0.5, locked at the first height 0.25.

- task.json: instruction, setup, scoring, run limit and fidelity notes
- README.md: run and score commands, every collider, how the handle and its pins are modelled, the scorer's conditions, the scripted demonstration, every simulation shortcut and estimate
- extend_suitcase_handle.py: scene, scorer and scripted demonstration
- case_runtime.py: the button's coupling to the two rails' lock pins and their holes, run before every physics step
- yam_parts.py, yam_joints.py: kit modules, copied unchanged

info.body: Hand-guiding a stopped collaborative arm to its service pose and teaching that pose, the way technicians set up and service robot cells. On a Franka Research 3 the arm moves by hand only while the Pilot-Grip's three-position Enabling Button is held at its middle position and its Guiding Button is pressed: released, the arm holds; squeezed through, as a startled hand would, it stops and needs a full release. So one gripper must keep its squeeze inside that narrow band while the same grip drags a seven-joint arm along its path, bring the hand down over the tool stand by feel, and let go there so the arm holds; then Teach, on the Pilot-Disc on top of the wrist, is pressed to store the pose. A picture shows where the hand should end, not how hard to squeeze on the way. Unlike moving a free object, the load being pulled is a robot that only moves while its own safety switch is held correctly. Full credit needs the arm brought within 1.5 cm and 5 degrees of the service pose with both buttons let go, Teach pressed with the arm still there, and every fingertip clear of the arm, held for 1 s; touching the bench or stand, a joint limit, or pushing the held arm scores 0. Dream-1 scored 0 in its 2,400 steps.

Adds a bimanual everyday task: open a food can with an ordinary two-handle rotary can opener. The handles are sprung open, so letting go stops the cut. Can and opener are real sizes; metal cutting is not simulated and is tracked by rule, as stated in the fidelity note.

info.body:
The robot mounts a turned shaft between the two 60-degree points of a bench centre, the way an inspector loads a shaft for a runout check. The bench centre's left point is fixed; the right point sits on a sprung sleeve that a hand lever draws back 10 mm. One hand holds the lever's ball knob down while the other lifts a 16 x 160 mm steel test shaft out of its V-blocks, sets one centre hole on the fixed point with the shaft turned, swings it into line about that point, and holds it while the lever is eased up so the sprung point enters the other centre hole. Full score needs each point in its seat (tip within 1 mm of the shaft's axis and 5.0-6.8 mm inside the end face), the lever at rest, both hands clear and the shaft still. A point left on a centre hole's protecting chamfer (a false runout reading) earns 0.5, a dropped shaft 0, and ramming the shaft against the sprung point instead of drawing it back with the lever caps the run at 0.5.

- README.md: run and score commands, the scoring rules, the scripted demonstration, every part's size and material, the sources for the bench centre and the centre holes, and the estimates still to measure
